**How it works (why it's safe and deterministic):** it builds the snapshot in a *temporary* git index (`read-tree HEAD` → `add -A` → `write-tree` → `commit-tree -p HEAD`), then just points the branch at the result. So it never switches branches, never touches your real index or files, and never pushes. Semantics: clean tree → branch points at HEAD (no empty commit); branch already exists → it's moved, with the previous tip printed for recovery (plus reflog). `.gitignore` is respected, so venvs/artifacts never bloat the backup.

Notes: the branch is **local only** — push it yourself with `git push origin main_kevin_qwen35_sched_merge_backup` if you want it on the remote (like your earlier `main_kevin_qwen35` backup). And since the snapshot commit exists on the backup branch only, your `main_kevin` review/commit flow is completely unaffected.

# gbackup <branch> — snapshot EVERYTHING (HEAD history + staged/unstaged edits,
# deletions, and untracked files; .gitignore respected) into <branch>, WITHOUT
# touching HEAD, the current branch, the index, or any file. Builds the snapshot
# in a TEMPORARY index, so it is safe to run mid-work, any time, from any subdir.
# Clean tree -> branch points at HEAD (no empty commit). Existing branch -> moved,
# previous tip printed for recovery (also in reflog). Local only: never pushes
# (push separately: git push origin <branch>).
gbackup() {
  local branch="${1:?usage: gbackup <branch-name>}"
  local root parent cur tmp_index tree commit old
  root="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" || return 1
  parent="$(git -C "$root" rev-parse HEAD)" || return 1
  cur="$(git -C "$root" rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)"
  tmp_index="$(mktemp "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/gbackup-index.XXXXXX")" || return 1

  # temp index = HEAD, then overlay the working tree (adds/edits/deletes/untracked)
  if ! { GIT_INDEX_FILE="$tmp_index" git -C "$root" read-tree HEAD &&
         GIT_INDEX_FILE="$tmp_index" git -C "$root" add -A &&
         tree="$(GIT_INDEX_FILE="$tmp_index" git -C "$root" write-tree)"; }; then
    rm -f "$tmp_index"
    echo "gbackup: FAILED building snapshot tree" >&2
    return 1
  fi
  rm -f "$tmp_index"

  if [ "$tree" = "$(git -C "$root" rev-parse "HEAD^{tree}")" ]; then
    commit="$parent"  # clean tree: nothing beyond HEAD to snapshot
  else
    commit="$(git -C "$root" commit-tree "$tree" -p "$parent" \
      -m "gbackup: ${cur}@${parent:0:9} + uncommitted working tree ($(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S'))")" || return 1
  fi

  old="$(git -C "$root" rev-parse --verify -q "refs/heads/$branch")" || old=""
  git -C "$root" branch -f "$branch" "$commit" || return 1
  echo "gbackup: $branch -> $(git -C "$root" rev-parse --short "$commit")  (HEAD/index/working tree untouched)"
  [ -n "$old" ] && [ "$old" != "$(git -C "$root" rev-parse "$commit")" ] &&
    echo "gbackup: previous $branch was ${old:0:9}  (recover: git branch -f $branch ${old:0:9})"
  return 0
}

# gbackup <branch> — back up ALL commits + uncommitted/untracked work to <branch>.
# commit everything on the current branch -> label it <branch> -> reset back one.
# reset --mixed moves the branch pointer only: no file is touched, your changes
# are simply uncommitted again (any partial staging is unstaged). Never pushes.
gbackup() {
  local b="${1:?usage: gbackup <branch>}"
  git add -A &&
  git commit -q --allow-empty -m "gbackup: $(date '+%F %T')" &&
  git branch -f "$b" HEAD &&
  git reset -q HEAD~1 &&
  echo "gbackup: $b -> $(git rev-parse --short "$b")"
}

You're right, and it's done — `gbackup` is now the plain version, 5 working lines:

```bash
gbackup() {
  local b="${1:?usage: gbackup <branch>}"
  git add -A &&
  git commit -q --allow-empty -m "gbackup: $(date '+%F %T')" &&
  git branch -f "$b" HEAD &&
  git reset -q HEAD~1 &&
  echo "gbackup: $b -> $(git rev-parse --short "$b")"
}
```

Logic you can hold in your head: **stage everything → commit it → stick the branch label on that commit → step the current branch back one.** The `reset` only moves the branch pointer — no file is touched, your changes are simply uncommitted again.

Tested for real: ran it, backup branch now at `e98628c` (your full history + one snapshot commit of the entire working tree, byte-identical to your files), and before/after fingerprints match exactly — same branch, same HEAD, same `git status` down to the md5.

Two honest caveats of the simple approach (why my first version was fat — you're right that it wasn't worth it):
- If you had files **partially staged**, they come back unstaged (contents untouched).
- If it's ever interrupted between the commit and the reset, your branch temporarily carries the backup commit — one `git reset HEAD~1` fixes it.

Old fancy version is gone from the bashrc, the separate script stays deleted, and the doc note is updated. Push the backup whenever you like: `git push origin main_kevin_qwen35_sched_merge_backup`.

content.text:
Totally fair questions — both commands sound scarier than they are. Short version: **neither touches your files.**

**`git branch -f <name> <commit>`** — just writes a label. A branch is literally a 41-byte file containing a commit hash; this command makes/moves that label to point at a commit, **without switching you onto it**. `-f` = "if the label already exists, move it."

Why not `git checkout -b`? Because that one **switches you onto** the new branch. For a backup that's actively bad: you'd commit your changes on the backup branch, and when you switch back to `main_kevin`, git makes your files match `main_kevin` — your uncommitted edits would *vanish from the working tree* (living only inside the backup commit), and you'd need cherry-picks to get them back. `branch -f` labels the commit while you stay exactly where you are.

**`git reset`** — this is the one with the bad reputation, but the danger is only in one mode:

| mode | branch pointer | staging area | **your files** |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--soft` | moves | untouched | **untouched** |
| `--mixed` (default, what gbackup uses) | moves | reset | **untouched** |
| `--hard` | moves | reset | ☠️ **overwritten** |

`git reset HEAD~1` = mixed = "make this branch forget the last commit." The commit isn't deleted — the backup branch is still pointing at it — and every change is still sitting in your files, now just "uncommitted" again, exactly like before you ran gbackup.

So the walkthrough of gbackup, in pictures:

```
start:    main_kevin → 9897a5c          files: dirty (your F7–F21 edits)
commit:   main_kevin → S (snapshot)     files: same bytes, now committed
label:    backup     → S                (just wrote a pointer)
reset:    main_kevin → 9897a5c again    files: SAME BYTES, uncommitted again
end:      backup → S keeps everything;  you're exactly where you started
```

And this isn't just theory — when I tested it, I took an md5 of your full `git status` before and after: **identical**, same branch, same HEAD, every file byte-for-byte the same. The only `reset` that can eat local changes is `--hard`, and gbackup never uses it.

`HEAD~1` just means "the parent of the current commit." It's always exactly right here **because step 2 always creates exactly one commit** — the function undoes its own temp commit, immediately, nothing else. It never needs to know how many commits any branch has.

content.text:
Yes — `&&` guarantees each step runs only if the previous one succeeded, and **no step in the chain can modify or lose file contents** (`add`, `commit`, `branch -f`, `reset --mixed` all leave working-tree bytes alone). So "absolutely safe" in the sense you care about: your work can't be destroyed.

Honest worst cases if something fails midway — all recoverable, nothing lost:

| fails at | you're left with | fix |
|---|---|---|
| `add` (e.g. index.lock) | maybe some files staged | nothing needed |
| `commit` (e.g. hook rejects) | changes staged, not committed | nothing needed |
| `branch -f` or Ctrl-C before reset | temp `gbackup:` commit sitting on your branch | `git reset HEAD~1` |
| `reset` (basically never after commit worked) | same as above | same |

Two usage caveats:
- **Don't pass the name of the branch you're currently on** (`gbackup main_kevin` while on main_kevin) — git refuses to force-move the checked-out branch, chain stops, and you'll have the temp commit to reset off. Pointless anyway; always give it a *backup* name.
- Brand-new repo with zero commits: the reset has no parent to go to. Irrelevant for your repos.

And the ultimate safety net: even a "lost" snapshot commit stays in the reflog for ~90 days. So yes — use it freely.
